acceleration into the generalized point mass assumption is only affected by the variation of velocity over the trajectory and best handled numerically.

# Problem 33

A projectile fired from a British 12 in. Mark IX naval gun had a muzzle velocity of  $2800\mathrm{ft / s}$  and was fired at a QE of 130 mil (Figure 9.9). Assuming a vacuum trajectory, at what deflection would the shot hit the ground?

Assume the firing is taking place at  $50^{\circ}$  south latitude and the round is being fired due north.

Answer:  $z = -75.8$  [ft]

# 9.5 Six Degree-of-Freedom (6 DOF) Trajectory

In keeping with our plan of increasing the complexity of our analyses to more closely approach the physical realities of projectile flight, we will now consider the projectile as a distributed mass. Since projectiles are relatively stiff structures, a 6 DOF model can adequately represent its position and attitude at any time. Each degree of freedom is tied to a coordinate necessary to completely describe the position of a body.

While this model is necessarily more complex than anything we have studied so far, the underlying physical principles remain the same. In the following work, we will use vectors (boldface, nonitalicized letters) in many of the derivations. We continue to do this because of the brevity and elegance of the notation.

In the equations that follow, we assume that the projectile is a rigid body of finite length with its mass distributed based on its geometry. This allows us to account for the effect of projectile attitude on drag and allows the full dynamics to come into play. We shall use direction cosines with respect to the projectile axis of symmetry (and thus a coordinate system with unit vectors  $\mathbf{i}$ ,  $\mathbf{j}$ , and  $\mathbf{k}$  that translates with the center of gravity (CG) but does not rotate and remains aligned with the projectile axis) as opposed to Eulerian angles (angles that are measured relative to the inertial coordinate system). This is illustrated in Figure 9.10.

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-01-18/00e670f9-7d2c-4ac2-9a7d-679d18d4a45f/befacf98597a10395d64fb2feebc2612ba54facbf321e44fc735e9a4f1f3034d.jpg)



FIGURE 9.10



Coordinate system for 6 DOF model.


Once again, we restate the equations of motion, which, for generality, includes a term for rocket propulsion of the projectile. However, because this force is usually assumed to be aligned with the longitudinal axis of the projectile, its effect on the motions we will study is uncoupled from the other motions and may be added in afterward. Consequently, we will ignore it in our further work:

$$
\mathbf {F} = m \mathbf {a} \tag {9.217}
$$

$$
m \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {V}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \boldsymbol {\Sigma} \mathbf {F} + m \mathbf {g} + m \boldsymbol {\Lambda} + \boldsymbol {\Sigma} \mathbf {R} _ {\mathrm {T}} \tag {9.218}
$$

Where  $m$  is the projectile mass;  $\mathbf{V}$  is the projectile velocity vector;  $t$  is the time;  $\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{V}}{\mathrm{d}t}$  is the vector acceleration;  $\Sigma \mathbf{F}$  is the vector sum of all aerodynamic forces;  $\mathbf{g}$  is the vector acceleration due to gravity;  $\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$  is the vector Coriolis acceleration due to rotation of the earth; and  $\Sigma \mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{T}}$  is the vector sum of all rocket thrust forces (to be ignored).

We can also write the equation for the conservation of angular momentum as

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {H}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \sum \mathbf {M} + \sum \mathbf {R} _ {\mathrm {M}} \tag {9.219}
$$

Where  $\mathbf{H}$  is the vector angular momentum of the projectile;  $\Sigma \mathbf{M}$  is the vector sum of all aerodynamic moments; and  $\Sigma \mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{M}}$  is the vector sum of all rocket thrust moments (to be ignored).

Because the projectile is assumed to be symmetric, every axis transverse to the longitudinal axis through the CG is a principal axis of inertia. The longitudinal axis itself is also, of course, a principal axis of inertia. The definition of the inertia tensor, which we will use, is

$$
\mathbf {I} = \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} I _ {x x} & - I _ {x y} & - I _ {x z} \\ - I _ {y x} & I _ {y y} & - I _ {y z} \\ - I _ {z x} & - I _ {z y} & I _ {z z} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.220}
$$

Here the diagonal terms are called the moments of inertia and the off-diagonal terms are called the products of inertia. We know that there is a rotation that can be applied to this tensor such that the off-diagonal elements go to zero. In this orientation, the axes are said to be principal axes of inertia, and the tensor is written as

$$
\mathbf {I} = \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} I _ {x} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & I _ {y} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & I _ {z} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.221}
$$

In our coordinate system, we shall define the unit vectors,  $\mathbf{i}$ ,  $\mathbf{j}$ , and  $\mathbf{k}$  so that they all lie along the principal axes of the projectile. Because of this unique situation, the total angular momentum of the projectile can be expressed as the sum of two vectors: the angular momentum about  $\mathbf{i}$  and the angular momentum about any axis perpendicular to  $\mathbf{i}$  through the CG. Since the  $\mathbf{i}$ -axis is what we usually call the polar axis, we will denote the polar moment of inertia as  $I_{\mathrm{P}}$ . With the symmetry of the projectile, the other moments of inertia

about axes perpendicular to  $\mathbf{i}$  are known as the transverse moments of inertia  $I_y = I_z = I_{\mathrm{T}}$ . We can then rewrite the inertia tensor as

$$
\mathbf {I} = \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} I _ {\mathrm {P}} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & I _ {\mathrm {T}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & I _ {\mathrm {T}} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.222}
$$

If a projectile is spinning at spin rate  $p$ , the angular momentum about the polar axis is defined as

$$
\mathbf {H} _ {\mathrm {P}} = I _ {\mathrm {P}} p \mathbf {i} \tag {9.223}
$$

The angular momentum about any transverse axis is defined as

$$
\mathbf {H} _ {\mathrm {T}} = I _ {\mathrm {T}} \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \tag {9.224}
$$

With this, we can write the total momentum vector as

$$
\mathbf {H} = I _ {\mathrm {P}} p \mathbf {i} + I _ {\mathrm {T}} \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \tag {9.225}
$$

By defining a specific angular momentum  $\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{H} / I_{\mathrm{T}}$  we can write

$$
\mathbf {h} = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \mathbf {i} + \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \tag {9.226}
$$

If we take the derivative of Equation 9.226 with respect to time, we get

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {h}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \dot {p} \mathbf {i} + \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t} + \left(\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) + \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} ^ {2} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t ^ {2}}\right) \tag {9.227}
$$

Since the cross product of a vector with itself is zero, we get

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {h}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \dot {p} \mathbf {i} + \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t} + \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} ^ {2} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t ^ {2}}\right) \tag {9.228}
$$

In anticipation of a later need, we shall take the dot product and cross product of vector  $\mathbf{h}$  with unit vector  $\mathbf{i}$  to get

$$
\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i} = \left[ \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \mathbf {i} + \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \right] \cdot \mathbf {i} = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \tag {9.229}
$$

$$
\mathbf {h} \times \mathbf {i} = \left[ \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \mathbf {i} + \left(\mathbf {i} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \right] \times \mathbf {i} = \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t} \tag {9.230}
$$

In Equations 9.229 and 9.230, we have used the orthogonality properties of vectors as follows:

$$
\mathbf {i} \cdot \mathbf {i} = 1
$$

$$
\mathbf {i} \cdot \mathbf {j} = \mathbf {i} \cdot \mathbf {k} = 0
$$

$$
\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {i} = 0
$$

$$
\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {j} = \mathbf {k} \rightarrow (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {j}) \times \mathbf {i} = (\mathbf {k}) \times \mathbf {i} = \mathbf {j} \therefore (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {j}) \times \mathbf {i} = \mathbf {j}
$$

We will now examine all the forces and then the moments acting on the projectile and combine them into Equations 9.218 and 9.219. We have discussed all these items in Chapter 7, so we shall simply refresh their meanings briefly and move on. The first force acting on the projectile is the drag force, which acts opposite to the velocity vector, so we have

$$
\operatorname {D r a g} \quad \text {f o r c e} = \mathbf {F} _ {\mathrm {D}} = - \frac {1}{2} \rho S C _ {\mathrm {D}} \mathbf {V} V \tag {9.231}
$$

The second force is the lift force, which we modified for our coordinate system as follows:

$$
\text {L i f t} = \mathbf {F} _ {\mathrm {L}} = - \frac {1}{2} \rho S C _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}} [ \mathbf {V} \times (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {V}) ] \tag {9.232}
$$

This equation contains a vector triple product in it that we replace with the relationship from vector algebra

$$
\mathbf {A} \times (\mathbf {B} \times \mathbf {C}) = (\mathbf {A} \cdot \mathbf {C}) \mathbf {B} - (\mathbf {A} \cdot \mathbf {B}) \mathbf {C} \tag {9.233}
$$

Which, for the product in Equation 9.232, can be written as

$$
\mathbf {V} \times (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {V}) = V ^ {2} \mathbf {i} - (\mathbf {V} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {V}
$$

When inserted into Equation 9.232, we have

$$
\text {L i f t} = \mathbf {F} _ {\mathrm {L}} = \frac {1}{2} \rho S C _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}} \left[ V ^ {2} \mathbf {i} - (\mathbf {V} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {V} \right] \tag {9.234}
$$

The next force is the Magnus force, brought on by the spin or roll of the projectile and taken from Equation 7.12:

$$
\text {M a g n u s} = \mathbf {F} _ {\mathrm {M}} = \frac {1}{2} \rho S V \left(\frac {p d}{V}\right) C _ {\mathrm {N p} \alpha} (\mathbf {V} \times \mathbf {i}) \tag {9.235}
$$

However, from Equation 9.229, we know that  $p = (I_{\mathrm{T}} / I_{\mathrm{P}})(\mathbf{h} \cdot \mathbf{i})$  and, from vector algebra,  $\mathbf{V} \times \mathbf{i} = -\mathbf{i} \times \mathbf{V}$ . Then, we can manipulate Equation 9.235 to the form

$$
\text {M a g n u s f o r c e} = \mathbf {F} _ {\mathrm {M}} = - \frac {1}{2} \rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N p} \alpha} \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {T}}}{I _ {\mathrm {P}}}\right) (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {V}) \tag {9.236}
$$

Next, we need to include the pitch-damping force from Equation 7.14, where we will write  $\mathbf{v}'$  as the unit vector along the velocity vector:

$$
\text {P i t c h - d a m p i n g f o r c e} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d \left(\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\dot {\alpha}}} \left(\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t} - \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {v} ^ {\prime}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \tag {9.237}
$$

If we assume  $\mathrm{dv}'/\mathrm{dt} = \mathrm{di}/\mathrm{dt}$  (this means that the rate at which the velocity vector is rotating to follow the curve of the trajectory is much smaller than the rate at which the axis of the projectile is moving) and we include Equation 9.230, we get a relation similar to Equation 7.17:

$$
\text {P i t c h - d a m p i n g f o r c e} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} \left(\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) + \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\dot {\alpha}}} \left(\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \tag {9.238}
$$

or by Equation 9.230,

$$
\text {P i t c h - d a m p i n g} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d \left(C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right) (\mathbf {h} \times \mathbf {i}) \tag {9.239}
$$

With all our forces now expressed in terms of our defined coefficients, we can divide Equation 9.218, omitting the rocket motor, by the projectile mass and inserting the coefficients to give

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {V}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \frac {\rho V S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} \mathbf {V} + \frac {\rho S C _ {\mathrm {L} \alpha}}{2 m} \left[ V ^ {2} \mathbf {i} - (\mathbf {V} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {V} \right] - \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N} \mathrm {p} \alpha}}{2 m} \binom {I _ {\mathrm {T}}} {I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {V}) \tag {9.240} \\ + \frac {\rho V S d \left(C _ {N _ {q}} + C _ {N _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 m} (\mathbf {h} \times \mathbf {i}) + \mathbf {g} + \boldsymbol {\Lambda} \\ \end{array}
$$

We will now examine the moments involved in Equation 9.219, the first of which is the spin-damping moment written as

$$
\text {S p i n - d a m p i n g} = \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {S}} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V ^ {2} S d \left(\frac {p d}{V}\right) C _ {\mathrm {I p}} \mathbf {i} \tag {9.241}
$$

However, if we again insert Equation 9.229 into the aforementioned equation, we get

$$
\text {S p i n - d a m p i n g m o m e n t} = \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {S}} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l} _ {\mathrm {p}}} \frac {I _ {\mathrm {T}}}{I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} \tag {9.242}
$$

The rolling moment comes from Equation 7.6 and is

$$
\text {R o l l i n g} = \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {R}} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {1 _ {\delta}} \mathbf {i} \tag {9.243}
$$

The overturning moment can be written from Equation 7.9 as

$$
\text {O v e r t u r n i n g m o m e n t} = \mathbf {M} _ {\alpha} = \frac {1}{2} \rho S d V C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}} (\mathbf {V} \times \mathbf {i}) \tag {9.244}
$$

The Magnus moment can be written from Equation 7.13, and, by using the relations of Equations 9.233 and 9.236, we get

$$
\text {M a g n u s m o m e n t} = \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha} = \frac {1}{2} \rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} \frac {I _ {\mathrm {T}}}{I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) [ \mathbf {V} - (\mathbf {V} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} ] \tag {9.245}
$$

We can obtain the pitch-damping moment by rewriting Equation 6.19 as well as using the relation of Equation 9.229 to get

$$
\text {P i t c h - d a m p i n g m o m e n t} = \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {q}} = \frac {1}{2} \rho V S d ^ {2} \left(C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}}\right) [ \mathbf {h} - (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} ] \tag {9.246}
$$

We can now place all these relations into Equation 9.219, again omitting the rocket term, to yield

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {H}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {S}} + \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {R}} + \mathbf {M} _ {\alpha} + \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha} + \mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {q}} \tag {9.247}
$$

Equation 9.247 can be changed to a more desirable form by dividing by  $I_{\mathrm{T}}$ , which yields

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {h}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {S}}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} + \frac {\mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {R}}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} + \frac {\mathbf {M} _ {\alpha}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} + \frac {\mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} + \frac {\mathbf {M} _ {\mathrm {q}}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \tag {9.248}
$$

This, in turn, may be rewritten by inserting the various moment equations derived earlier as

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {h}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\rho V S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l p}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} + \frac {\rho V ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {\mathrm {l} _ {\delta}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \mathbf {i} + \frac {\rho V S d C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} (\mathbf {V} \times \mathbf {i}) \tag {9.249} \\ + \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M _ {p} \alpha}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) [ \mathbf {V} - (\mathbf {V} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} ] + \frac {\rho V S d ^ {2} (C _ {\mathrm {M _ {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {M _ {\dot {\alpha}}}})}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} [ \mathbf {h} - (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} ] \\ \end{array}
$$

Note that the equations of motion are highly coupled to one another, and the reason we call the model a 6 DOF is readily apparent. When we break the equations up into their individual components, we have six equations and six unknowns  $(x,y,z,p,\alpha ,$  and  $\beta)$ . Let us recall that the  $x$ -,  $y$ -, and  $z$ -axes are axes fixed to the earth, independent of the projectile, while  $\mathbf{i}$  is the unit vector along the axis of symmetry of the projectile and has components along the  $x,y,z$  earth axes, and  $p$ ,  $\alpha$ , and  $\beta$  are the spin rate, pitch, and yaw angles, respectively. For convenience and clarity, and to facilitate analysis, we will relabel the  $x,y,z$  unit vectors (normally  $\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},$  and  $\mathbf{k}$ ) as  $\mathbf{e}_1,\mathbf{e}_2,$  and  $\mathbf{e}_3$ , respectively, letting the subscripts denote the  $x$ -,  $y$ -,  $z$ -axes in that order (see Figure 9.10). Then, in terms of components in the earth-fixed system,

$$
\mathbf {h} = h _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + h _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + h _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.250}
$$

$$
\mathbf {i} = i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.251}
$$

$$
\mathbf {V} = V _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + V _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + V _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.252}
$$

$$
\mathbf {W} = W _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + W _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + W _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.253}
$$

We shall also define

$$
\mathbf {v} = \mathbf {V} - \mathbf {W} = \left(V _ {1} - W _ {1}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(V _ {2} - W _ {2}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \left(V _ {3} - W _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.254}
$$

and further defining

$$
v _ {1} = \left(V _ {1} - W _ {1}\right), \quad v _ {2} = \left(V _ {2} - W _ {2}\right), \quad v _ {3} = \left(V _ {3} - W _ {3}\right) \tag {9.255}
$$

and

$$
v = \sqrt {v _ {1} ^ {2} + v _ {2} ^ {2} + v _ {3} ^ {2}} \tag {9.256}
$$

We can insert the definition for  $\mathbf{v}$  in place of  $\mathbf{V}$  in Equations 9.245 and 9.249 to yield

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {V}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \frac {\rho v S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} \mathbf {v} + \frac {\rho S C _ {\mathrm {L} \alpha}}{2 m} \left[ v ^ {2} \mathbf {i} - (\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {v} \right] - \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N p} \alpha}}{2 m} \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {T}}}{I _ {\mathrm {P}}}\right) (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {v}) \tag {9.257} \\ + \frac {\rho v S d \left(C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\alpha}}\right)}{2 m} (\mathbf {h} \times \mathbf {i}) + \mathbf {g} + \boldsymbol {\Lambda} \\ \end{array}
$$

and

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {h}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l p}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} + \frac {\rho v ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {\mathrm {l} \delta}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \mathbf {i} + \frac {\rho v S d C _ {\mathrm {M} \alpha}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} (\mathbf {v} \times \mathbf {i}) \tag {9.258} \\ + \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {P}}} (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) [ \mathbf {v} - (\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} ] + \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} (C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}})}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} [ \mathbf {h} - (\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} ] \\ \end{array}
$$

Our goal is to examine Equations 9.257 and 9.258 and break each into three equations, one for each coordinate direction (actually for the acceleration in each coordinate direction). But before we attempt to break Equations 9.257 and 9.258 into their components, it will be best to solve for some of the vector quantities that occur in them. Beginning with the second term of Equation 9.257, we can, with appropriate vector multiplication, obtain

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {v} = \left(v _ {1} ^ {2} i _ {1} + v _ {1} v _ {2} i _ {2} + v _ {1} v _ {3} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(v _ {1} v _ {2} i _ {1} + v _ {2} ^ {2} i _ {2} + v _ {2} v _ {3} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} \\ + \left(v _ {1} v _ {3} i _ {1} + v _ {2} v _ {3} i _ {2} + v _ {3} ^ {2} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.259} \\ \end{array}
$$

Another useful relation is

$$
\left(\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}\right) = \left(v _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + v _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + v _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \cdot \left(i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \tag {9.260}
$$

or

$$
\left(\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}\right) = v _ {1} i _ {1} + v _ {2} i _ {2} + v _ {3} i _ {3} \tag {9.261}
$$

However, we can show that

$$
\cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} = \frac {(\mathbf {v} \cdot \dot {\mathbf {i}})}{v} = \frac {v _ {1} i _ {1} + v _ {2} i _ {2} + v _ {3} i _ {3}}{v} \tag {9.262}
$$

The next relations in Equation 9.257 are

$$
\left(\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}\right) = h _ {1} i _ {1} + h _ {2} i _ {2} + h _ {3} i _ {3} \tag {9.263}
$$

and

$$
(\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {v}) = \left| \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \\ i _ {1} & i _ {2} & i _ {3} \\ v _ {1} & v _ {2} & v _ {3} \end{array} \right| = (i _ {2} v _ {3} - i _ {3} v _ {2}) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + (i _ {3} v _ {1} - i _ {1} v _ {3}) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + (i _ {1} v _ {2} - i _ {2} v _ {1}) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.264}
$$

Now, also in Equation 9.257 is the term

$$
(\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {v}) = \left(h _ {1} i _ {1} + h _ {2} i _ {2} + h _ {3} i _ {3}\right) \left[ \left(i _ {2} v _ {3} - i _ {3} v _ {2}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(i _ {3} v _ {1} - i _ {1} v _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \left(i _ {1} v _ {2} - i _ {2} v _ {1}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \tag {9.265}
$$

But with the fact that  $(\mathbf{h}\cdot \mathbf{i}) = I_{\mathrm{P}}p / I_{\mathrm{T}}$  as shown earlier, then we can write

$$
(\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) (\mathbf {i} \times \mathbf {v}) = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} (i _ {2} v _ {3} - i _ {3} v _ {2}) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} (i _ {3} v _ {1} - i _ {1} v _ {3}) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} (i _ {1} v _ {2} - i _ {2} v _ {1}) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.266}
$$

Another relation we have to deal with is

$$
(\mathbf {h} \times \mathbf {i}) = \left| \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \\ h _ {1} & h _ {2} & h _ {3} \\ i _ {1} & i _ {2} & i _ {3} \end{array} \right| = (h _ {2} i _ {3} - h _ {3} i _ {2}) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + (h _ {3} i _ {1} - h _ {1} i _ {3}) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + (h _ {1} i _ {2} - h _ {2} i _ {1}) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.267}
$$

The next relation we generate with the help of Equation 9.229 is

$$
(\mathbf {h} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.268}
$$

In Equation 9.258, we need

$$
(\mathbf {v} \times \mathbf {i}) = \left| \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \\ v _ {1} & v _ {2} & v _ {3} \\ i _ {1} & i _ {2} & i _ {3} \end{array} \right| = (i _ {3} v _ {2} - i _ {2} v _ {3}) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + (i _ {1} v _ {3} - i _ {3} v _ {1}) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + (i _ {2} v _ {1} - i _ {1} v _ {2}) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.269}
$$

And finally in Equation 9.258,

$$
(\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} = \left(v _ {1} i _ {1} + v _ {2} i _ {2} + v _ {3} i _ {3}\right) \left(i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \tag {9.270}
$$

or

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\mathbf {v} \cdot \mathbf {i}) \mathbf {i} = \left(v _ {1} i _ {1} ^ {2} + v _ {2} i _ {1} i _ {2} + v _ {3} i _ {1} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(v _ {1} i _ {1} i _ {2} + v _ {2} i _ {2} ^ {2} + v _ {3} i _ {2} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} \\ + \left(v _ {1} i _ {1} i _ {3} + v _ {2} i _ {2} i _ {3} + v _ {3} i _ {3} ^ {2}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.271} \\ \end{array}
$$

Let us now look at Equation 9.257 with all the vector quantities broken into their components

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {1}}{\mathrm {d} t} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {2}}{\mathrm {d} t} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {3}}{\mathrm {d} t} \mathbf {e} _ {3} = - \frac {\rho v S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} \left(v _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + v _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + v _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \\ + \frac {\rho S C _ {L \alpha}}{2 m} \left[ v ^ {2} i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + v ^ {2} i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + v ^ {2} i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} - v \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \left(v _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + v _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + v _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \right] \\ - \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N} \mathrm {p} \alpha}}{2 m} \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {T}}}{I _ {\mathrm {P}}}\right) \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) \left[ \left(v _ {3} i _ {2} - v _ {2} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(v _ {1} i _ {3} - v _ {3} i _ {1}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \left(v _ {2} i _ {1} - v _ {1} i _ {2}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \tag {9.272} \\ + \frac {\rho v S d \left(C _ {N _ {q}} + C _ {N _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 m} \left[ \left(h _ {2} i _ {3} - h _ {3} i _ {2}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(h _ {3} i _ {1} - h _ {1} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \left(h _ {1} i _ {2} - h _ {2} i _ {1}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \\ + g _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + g _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + g _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} + \Lambda_ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \Lambda_ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \Lambda_ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \\ \end{array}
$$

Similarly, let us perform the same operation on Equation 9.258

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {1}}{\mathrm {d} t} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {2}}{\mathrm {d} t} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {3}}{\mathrm {d} t} \mathbf {e} _ {3} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} C _ {1 p}}{2 I _ {P}} \left(\frac {I _ {P} p}{I _ {T}}\right) \left(i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \\ + \frac {\rho v ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {1 \delta}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left(i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) + \frac {\rho v S d C _ {\mathrm {M} \alpha}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ \left(v _ {2} i _ {3} - v _ {3} i _ {2}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(v _ {3} i _ {1} - v _ {1} i _ {3}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \left(v _ {1} i _ {2} - v _ {2} i _ {1}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \\ + \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M p a}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {P}}} \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) \left[ \left(v _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + v _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + v _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) - v \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \left(i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \right] \\ + \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} \left(C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}}\right)}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ \left(h _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + h _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + h _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) \left(i _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3}\right) \right] \tag {9.273} \\ \end{array}
$$

We will first operate on Equation 9.272 by collecting all the terms with the unit vectors  $\mathbf{e}_1$ , then  $\mathbf{e}_2$  and  $\mathbf{e}_3$  and by putting them into the equations for linear and angular momentum:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {1}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \frac {\rho v S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} v _ {1} + \frac {p S C _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}}}{2 m} \left[ v ^ {2} i _ {1} - v v _ {1} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \right] - \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} p}{2 m} (v _ {3} i _ {2} - v _ {2} i _ {3}) \\ + \frac {\rho v S d \left(C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 m} \left(h _ {2} i _ {3} - h _ {3} i _ {2}\right) + g _ {1} + \Lambda_ {1} \tag {9.274} \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {2}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \frac {\rho v S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} v _ {2} + \frac {p S C _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}}}{2 m} \left[ v ^ {2} i _ {2} - v v _ {2} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \right] - \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} p}{2 m} \left(v _ {1} i _ {3} - v _ {3} i _ {1}\right) \\ + \frac {\rho v S d \left(C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 m} \left(h _ {3} i _ {1} - h _ {1} i _ {3}\right) + g _ {2} + \Lambda_ {2} \tag {9.275} \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {3}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \frac {\rho v S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} v _ {3} + \frac {p S C _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}}}{2 m} \left[ v ^ {2} i _ {3} - v v _ {3} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \right] - \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} p}{2 m} (v _ {2} i _ {1} - v _ {1} i _ {2}) \\ + \frac {\rho v S d \left(C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 m} \left(h _ {1} i _ {2} - h _ {2} i _ {1}\right) + g _ {3} + \Lambda_ {3} \tag {9.276} \\ \end{array}
$$

Next is Equation 9.273, where the same procedure will be followed:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {1}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l p}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {1} + \frac {\rho v ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {\mathrm {l} _ {\delta}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {1} + \frac {\rho v S d C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left(v _ {2} i _ {3} - v _ {3} i _ {2}\right) \tag {9.277} \\ + \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M p a}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ v _ {1} - v i _ {1} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \right] + \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} \left(C _ {\mathrm {M q}} + C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ h _ {1} - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) i _ {1} \right] \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {2}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l p}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {2} + \frac {\rho v ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {\mathrm {l} \delta}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {2} + \frac {\rho v S d C _ {\mathrm {M} \alpha}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left(v _ {3} i _ {1} - v _ {1} i _ {3}\right) \tag {9.278} \\ + \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ v _ {2} - v i _ {2} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \right] + \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} \left(C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\dot {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ h _ {2} - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) i _ {2} \right] \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {3}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l p}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {3} + \frac {\rho v ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {\mathrm {l} _ {\delta}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {3} + \frac {\rho v S d C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left(v _ {1} i _ {2} - v _ {2} i _ {1}\right) \tag {9.279} \\ + \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M} \mathrm {p} \alpha} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ v _ {3} - v i _ {3} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}} \right] + \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} \left(C _ {\mathrm {M} \mathrm {q}} + C _ {\mathrm {M} \dot {\alpha}}\right)}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \left[ h _ {3} - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) i _ {3} \right] \\ \end{array}
$$

We can simplify Equations 9.274 through 9.279 considerably by defining the following coefficients:

$$
\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {D}} = \frac {\rho v S C _ {\mathrm {D}}}{2 m} \quad \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l p}} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {l p}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}}
$$

$$
\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}} = \frac {\rho S C _ {\mathrm {L} _ {\alpha}}}{2 m} \quad \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l} _ {\delta}} = \frac {\rho v ^ {2} S d \delta_ {\mathrm {F}} C _ {\mathrm {l} _ {\delta}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}}
$$

$$
\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} = \frac {\rho S d C _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} p}{2 m} \quad \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}} = \frac {\rho v S d C _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}}}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}}
$$

$$
\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N _ {q}}} = \frac {\rho v S d \left(C _ {\mathrm {N _ {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {N _ {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 m} \quad \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M _ {p \alpha}}} = \frac {\rho S d ^ {2} C _ {\mathrm {M _ {p \alpha}}} p}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}}
$$

$$
\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M _ {q}}} = \frac {\rho v S d ^ {2} \left(C _ {\mathrm {M _ {q}}} + C _ {\mathrm {M _ {\alpha}}}\right)}{2 I _ {\mathrm {T}}}
$$

With these coefficients, we can write Equations 9.274 through 9.276 in a more compact form:

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {1}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {D}} v _ {1} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {L} \alpha} \left(v ^ {2} i _ {1} - v v _ {1} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}}\right) - \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} \left(v _ {3} i _ {2} - v _ {2} i _ {3}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} \left(h _ {2} i _ {3} - h _ {3} i _ {2}\right) + g _ {1} + \Lambda_ {1} \tag {9.280}
$$

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {2}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {D}} v _ {2} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {L} \alpha} \left(v ^ {2} i _ {2} - v v _ {2} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}}\right) - \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} \left(v _ {1} i _ {3} - v _ {3} i _ {1}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} \left(h _ {3} i _ {1} - h _ {1} i _ {3}\right) + g _ {2} + \Lambda_ {2} \tag {9.281}
$$

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} V _ {3}}{\mathrm {d} t} = - \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {D}} v _ {3} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {L} \alpha} \left(v ^ {2} i _ {3} - v v _ {3} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}}\right) - \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} \left(v _ {2} i _ {1} - v _ {1} i _ {2}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {N} _ {\mathrm {q}}} \left(h _ {1} i _ {2} - h _ {2} i _ {1}\right) + g _ {3} + \Lambda_ {3} \tag {9.282}
$$

We can do the same with Equations 9.277 through 9.279:

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {1}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \left(\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l p}} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l} \delta}\right) i _ {1} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}} \left(v _ {2} i _ {3} - v _ {3} i _ {2}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} \left(v _ {1} - v i _ {1} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathbf {q}}} \left[ h _ {1} - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) i _ {1} \right] \tag {9.283}
$$

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {2}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \left(\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l p}} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l \delta}}\right) i _ {2} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\alpha}} \left(v _ {3} i _ {1} - v _ {1} i _ {3}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathrm {p} \alpha}} \left(v _ {2} - v i _ {2} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} _ {\mathbf {q}}} \left[ h _ {2} - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) i _ {2} \right] \tag {9.284}
$$

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} h _ {3}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \left(\tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l p}} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {l s}}\right) i _ {3} + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} \alpha} \left(v _ {1} i _ {2} - v _ {2} i _ {1}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M} \mathrm {p} \alpha} \left(v _ {3} - v i _ {3} \cos \alpha_ {\mathrm {t}}\right) + \tilde {C} _ {\mathrm {M q}} \left[ h _ {3} - \left(\frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}}\right) i _ {3} \right] \tag {9.285}
$$

Now that we have the six coupled equations for our six accelerations, we would like to determine the position of the projectile in space and time. We do this by creating a vector  $\mathbf{X}$  to the center of mass of the projectile. If we note that  $\mathbf{X} = [x\mathbf{e}_1 + y\mathbf{e}_2 + z\mathbf{e}_3]$  in the earth-fixed coordinate system, then we can break the individual components into

$$
x = x _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} V _ {1} \mathrm {d} t \tag {9.286}
$$

$$
y = y _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} V _ {2} \mathrm {d} t \tag {9.287}
$$

$$
z = z _ {0} + \int_ {0} ^ {t} V _ {3} \mathrm {d} t \tag {9.288}
$$

Recognize that when firing a long-range weapon, we usually do so with grid coordinates on a map of the earth. A map is, in theory, created by peeling the geometry off a globe. Thus, the coordinates and distances are correct in the downrange and cross-range directions  $(x$  and  $z$ ). However, the altitude  $y$  has to be corrected for the curvature of the earth. This is depicted with the applicable equations in Figure 9.11. A similar rotation occurs with the gravity vector as depicted in Figure 9.12.

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-01-18/00e670f9-7d2c-4ac2-9a7d-679d18d4a45f/0364595eb45ecf6517be5ce341fcb9b74426bdc92c890b230c103089c30fec11.jpg)


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-01-18/00e670f9-7d2c-4ac2-9a7d-679d18d4a45f/aa9a624193a492b5bfbb4c312e6a4fa17a927ffb9e75dba8d75feceecaf750fe.jpg)


$$
E _ {2} \cos \theta \approx E _ {2}
$$

$$
E _ {2} \cos \theta = 2 R \sin^ {2} \frac {\theta}{2}
$$

$$
2 R \sin^ {2} \frac {\theta}{2} \approx 2 R \frac {\theta^ {2}}{4}
$$

$$
E _ {2} \approx \frac {R \theta^ {2}}{2} = \frac {R}{2} \frac {x ^ {2}}{R ^ {2}} \rightarrow E _ {2} \approx \frac {x ^ {2}}{2 R}
$$


FIGURE 9.11



Altitude error over long trajectories.


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-01-18/00e670f9-7d2c-4ac2-9a7d-679d18d4a45f/787ea57c7678b9c0aa85e83fe80d0b28b8ed86598d51c663cee4527c695fe6c7.jpg)



FIGURE 9.12 Rotation of the gravity vector due to earth curvature and associated equations.


With this relationship, we can write the projectile position vector in earth coordinates as

$$
\mathbf {E} \approx \left[ E _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + E _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + E _ {3} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] = \left[ x \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(y + \frac {x ^ {2}}{2 R}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + z \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} x \\ y + \frac {x ^ {2}}{2 R} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.289}
$$

Where  $R$  is the average radius of the earth, taken to be 6,951,844 yards or 6,356,766 m. The use of earth coordinates is recommended at ranges beyond about 2000 yards (at 2000 yards, there is a 10.36 in. difference in height [1]). Furthermore, the acceleration of gravity varies with altitude (and, in fact, latitude and longitude as well), and we need to consider this.

To complete the equations of motion, we must consider the form of the Coriolis acceleration vector. We have discussed this extensively previously so we shall simply write the components of this vector as

$$
\Lambda_ {1} = 2 \Omega \left(- V _ {2} \cos L \sin A Z - V _ {3} \sin L\right) \tag {9.290}
$$

$$
\Lambda_ {2} = 2 \Omega \left(V _ {1} \cos L \sin A Z + V _ {3} \cos L \cos A Z\right) \tag {9.291}
$$

$$
\Lambda_ {3} = 2 \Omega \left(V _ {1} \sin L - V _ {2} \cos L \cos A Z\right) \tag {9.292}
$$

or as a vector

$$
\boldsymbol {\Lambda} = \left[ \begin{array}{l} \Lambda_ {1} \\ \Lambda_ {2} \\ \Lambda_ {3} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} \end{array} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] = 2 \Omega \left[ \begin{array}{c} - V _ {2} \cos L \sin A Z - V _ {3} \sin L \\ V _ {1} \cos L \sin A Z + V _ {3} \cos L \cos A Z \\ V _ {1} \sin L - V _ {2} \cos L \cos A Z \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} \\ & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.293}
$$

We now have the differential equations of motion but need initial conditions to solve them. Let us examine the projectile at the instant of muzzle exit without worrying about how it attained its state of motion there (this is the job of the interior ballistician). We shall define the initial tube angle in azimuth and elevation as  $\theta_0$  and  $\phi_0$ , respectively. Then, our initial velocity vector can be defined as

$$
\mathbf {V} _ {0} = \left[ \begin{array}{l} \Lambda_ {1} \\ \Lambda_ {2} \\ \Lambda_ {3} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} \end{array} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] = V _ {0} \left[ \begin{array}{c} \cos \phi_ {0} \cos \theta_ {0} \\ \sin \phi_ {0} \cos \theta_ {0} \\ \sin \theta_ {0} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} \end{array} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \tag {9.294}
$$

And, if we also take the wind into account, we have

$$
\mathbf {v} _ {0} = \mathbf {V} _ {0} - \mathbf {W} _ {0} = \left[ \begin{array}{l} v _ {1 _ {0}} \\ v _ {2 _ {0}} \\ v _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{l} V _ {1 _ {0}} - W _ {1 _ {0}} \\ V _ {2 _ {0}} - W _ {2 _ {0}} \\ V _ {3 _ {0}} - W _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.295}
$$

Here the usual relationships for these vectors apply. These are

$$
V _ {0} = \sqrt {V _ {1 _ {0}} ^ {2} + V _ {2 _ {0}} ^ {2} + V _ {3 _ {0}} ^ {2}} \tag {9.296}
$$

$$
v _ {0} = \sqrt {v _ {1 _ {0}} ^ {2} + v _ {2 _ {0}} ^ {2} + v _ {3 _ {0}} ^ {2}} \tag {9.297}
$$

The initial orientations of the body-fixed unit vectors in the earth-fixed system are

$$
\mathbf {i} _ {0} = i _ {1 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + i _ {2 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + i _ {3 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {3} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} i _ {1 _ {0}} \\ i _ {2 _ {0}} \\ i _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \cos (\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}) \cos (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) \\ \sin (\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}) \cos (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) \\ \sin (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.298}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathbf {j} _ {0} = j _ {1 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + j _ {2 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + j _ {3 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {3} = \left[ \begin{array}{l} j _ {1 _ {0}} \\ j _ {2 _ {0}} \\ j _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} & \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \\ = \frac {1}{\sqrt {Q}} \left[ \begin{array}{l} - \cos^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \sin \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) \cos \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) \\ \cos^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \cos^ {2} \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) + \sin^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \\ - \sin \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \cos \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \sin \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) \end{array} \right] [ \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} ] \tag {9.299} \\ \end{array}
$$

$$
\mathbf {k} _ {0} = k _ {1 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + k _ {2 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + k _ {3 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {3} = \left[ \begin{array}{c} k _ {1 _ {0}} \\ k _ {2 _ {0}} \\ k _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] = \frac {1}{\sqrt {Q}} \left[ \begin{array}{c} - \sin (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) \\ 0 \\ \cos (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) \cos (\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}) \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c} \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] (9. 3 0 0)
$$

In the aforementioned equations,  $\alpha_0$  and  $\beta_0$  are the initial pitch and yaw angles, respectively, of the projectile. Thus, they directly add to the weapon azimuth and elevation angles. We define quantity  $Q$  following McCoy [1] as

$$
Q = \sin^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) + \cos^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \cos^ {2} \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) \tag {9.301}
$$

If we now consider the rotation  $(\omega)_{ijk}$  of the projectile about its axis of symmetry (thus relative to the i-j-k triad) and we define an arbitrary initial projectile rotation as

$$
\left(\boldsymbol {\omega} _ {0}\right) _ {i j k} = \omega_ {i _ {0}} \mathbf {i} _ {0} + \omega_ {j _ {0}} \mathbf {j} _ {0} + \omega_ {k _ {0}} \mathbf {k} _ {0} \tag {9.302}
$$

Here this initial angular velocity is dependent upon the initial orientation of the unit vector  $\mathrm{i}_0$ . Then, the initial velocity of the unit vector can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i} _ {0}}{\mathrm {d} t} = (\boldsymbol {\omega} _ {0}) _ {i j k} \times \mathbf {i} _ {0} = \left| \begin{array}{c c c} \mathbf {i} _ {0} & \mathbf {j} _ {0} & \mathbf {k} _ {0} \\ \omega_ {i _ {0}} & \omega_ {j _ {0}} & \omega_ {k _ {0}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{array} \right| = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \omega_ {k _ {0}} \mathbf {j} _ {0} - \omega_ {j _ {0}} \mathbf {k} _ {0} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} \\ \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} \\ \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] [ \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} ] \\ = \left[ \begin{array}{l} \omega_ {k _ {0}} j _ {1 _ {0}} - \omega_ {j _ {0}} k _ {1 _ {0}} \\ \omega_ {k _ {0}} j _ {2 _ {0}} - \omega_ {j _ {0}} k _ {2 _ {0}} \\ \omega_ {k _ {0}} j _ {3 _ {0}} - \omega_ {j _ {0}} k _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] [ \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} ] \tag {9.303} \\ \end{array}
$$

Note that Equation 9.303 is a tensor equation. Tensors are higher-order vectors but can be treated the same. If we insert the results of Equations 9.299 and 9.300 into the aforementioned equation, we get

$$
\dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {Q}} = \left[ \omega_ {j _ {0}} \sin (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) - \omega_ {k _ {0}} \cos^ {2} (\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}) \sin (\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}) \cos (\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}) \right] \tag {9.304}
$$

$$
\dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {Q}} = \left[ \omega_ {k _ {0}} \cos^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \cos^ {2} \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) + \omega_ {k _ {0}} \sin^ {2} \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \right] \tag {9.305}
$$

$$
\dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} = \frac {1}{\sqrt {Q}} \left[ - \omega_ {j _ {0}} \cos \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \cos \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) - \omega_ {k _ {0}} \sin \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \cos \left(\theta_ {0} + \beta_ {0}\right) \sin \left(\phi_ {0} + \alpha_ {0}\right) \right] \tag {9.306}
$$

Continuing with our statement of the initial conditions, a positive pitch rotates the nose of the projectile upward and a positive yaw rotates the nose to the left as viewed from the rear. The initial value of the modified angular momentum vector is given by

$$
\mathbf {h} _ {0} = \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p _ {0}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} \mathbf {i} _ {0} + \left(\mathbf {i} _ {0} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i} _ {0}}{\mathrm {d} t}\right) \tag {9.307}
$$

We can rewrite  $\mathrm{d}\mathbf{i}_0 / \mathrm{d}t$  as

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i} _ {0}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.308}
$$

Which then allows us to write

$$
\mathbf {i} _ {0} \times \frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {i} _ {0}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \left| \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} \mathbf {e} _ {2} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \\ i _ {1 _ {0}} i _ {2 _ {0}} i _ {3 _ {0}} \\ \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right| = \left(i _ {2 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} - i _ {3 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {1} + \left(i _ {3 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} - i _ {1 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {2} + \left(i _ {1 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} - i _ {2 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}}\right) \mathbf {e} _ {3} \tag {9.309}
$$

We can then incorporate Equation 9.309 into Equation 9.307 to yield

$$
\mathbf {h} _ {0} = \left[ \begin{array}{l} h _ {1 _ {0}} \\ h _ {2 _ {0}} \\ h _ {3 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} \end{array} \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{l} \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p _ {0}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {1 _ {0}} + i _ {2 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} - i _ {3 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} \\ \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p _ {0}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {2 _ {0}} + i _ {3 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} - i _ {1 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {3 _ {0}} \\ \frac {I _ {\mathrm {P}} p _ {0}}{I _ {\mathrm {T}}} i _ {3 _ {0}} + i _ {1 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {2 _ {0}} - i _ {2 _ {0}} \dot {i} _ {1 _ {0}} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {e} _ {1} & \mathbf {e} _ {2} \end{array} \begin{array}{l} \mathbf {e} _ {3} \end{array} \right] \tag {9.310}
$$

Here the initial value of the spin rate  $p_0$  is determined by the axial velocity and the twist rate  $n$  (in calibers per revolution) of the weapon through  $p_0 = 2\pi V_0 / nd$ . We have thus completed all the initial conditions necessary to perform the calculation.

As we will discuss in a later section, the motion of the motion can be characterized as epicyclic. The tip of a vector drawn from the CG of the projectile to the nose will trace out a curve that contains two cyclic modes: a fast mode, known as nutation, and a slow mode, known as precession. If the round is stable, these modes will eventually damp down to near zero, leaving only some movement because of nonlinear forces and moments. We shall explore this more later.

Some other terms come up in the succeeding sections that require definitions. Since they are essential to the understanding of trajectories, we will define them now.

The yaw of a projectile of repose is the yaw created by the action of gravity on the projectile as it attempts to follow its trajectory curve. As stated earlier, the nose of the projectile is usually above the trajectory. There is then a net aerodynamic force through the CP which wants to rotate the nose up. With a right-hand spinning projectile, this results in a yaw of the nose to the right. This is called the yaw of repose.

Failure to trail is a situation that arises when the base of the projectile does not follow the nose (it flies base first after maximum ordinate). This is depicted in Figure 9.13.

The trail angle is the quadrant elevation angle (particular to a gun, projectile, and charge combination) above which the projectile will not turn over and will fail to trail.

We can summarize this section by saying that for a rigid projectile, the 6 DOF model is as accurate as one can get to the trajectories. If the model yields an inaccurate answer, the problem is usually a wrong assumption in the metrology, initial conditions, or projectile mass properties. Lastly, the only practical method of solving these equations is by numerical methods, and, with the speed of computers today, the codes run very efficiently and quickly. This last statement makes it difficult to generate meaningful problems for the interested reader. We have endeavored to create useful exercises by stipulating a large number of conditions and requiring the reader to examine the accelerations of the projectile at a point in space.

# Problem 34

A British bomber is flying at a speed of  $200\mathrm{mph}$  in still air. If the 0.303 in. machine guns are fired sideways, calculate the axial acceleration vector and the angular acceleration vector acting on the projectile through use of the 6 DOF equations if the projectile is

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-01-18/00e670f9-7d2c-4ac2-9a7d-679d18d4a45f/4f8ce7872501ff569cd098d8e7970cd86c5d485a4f2310709ad99dd22a0f2d7c.jpg)



FIGURE 9.13 Projectile that has failed to trail.


1. Fired to the right Answer:

$$
\mathbf {a} = \left[ - 1 3 7 6 \mathbf {e} _ {1} + 5. 8 9 \mathbf {e} _ {2} - 1 1 8 4 \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \left[ \frac {\mathrm {f t}}{\mathrm {s}} \right]
$$

$$
\frac {\mathrm {d} \mathbf {h}}{\mathrm {d} t} = \left[ 3 9. 8 5 \mathbf {e} _ {1} - 3 5, 9 2 2 \mathbf {e} _ {2} - 2. 4 5 \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \left[ \frac {\mathrm {r a d}}{\mathrm {s} ^ {2}} \right]
$$

2. Fired to the left Answer:

$$
\mathbf {a} = \left[ - 1 3 7 6 \mathbf {e} _ {1} + 7 0. 2 9 \mathbf {e} _ {2} - 1 1 8 4 \mathbf {e} _ {3} \right] \left[ \frac {\mathrm {f t}}{\mathrm {s} ^ {2}} \right]
$$

$$
